81.quote_or_event: Every gurdwara keeps a langar, a communal kitchen where all who come are fed sitting together in a line, a practice that grew up as a protest against caste; the Gurus also praised the life of the ordinary householder over withdrawal from the world.
81.explanation: Sikhism rejects renunciation and locates the religious life in the household, and its central institution of hospitality, the langar, turns every congregation into a host that feeds anyone who arrives.
81.tie_back: As Valluvar says the whole point of keeping a home is to cherish guests, the Sikh householder and the gurdwara exist in large part to feed the stranger.
81.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, articles on langar and Sikh practice, and on Guru Amar Das (paraphrase)
81._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on household life justified by hospitality; the langar is a communal institution of the congregation rather than the private household the Kural describes.

82.quote_or_event: Guru Amar Das made it a rule that anyone who wished to see him had first to eat in the langar, sitting alongside everyone else; tradition holds that even the Mughal emperor Akbar ate in the casteless langar before meeting him.
82.explanation: The third Guru made shared eating the precondition of every meeting, so that no one, however powerful, could be received while others went unfed or were kept apart.
82.tie_back: It enacts the Kural's refusal to eat alone while a guest waits outside: at the Guru's court no one dined privately while others were left out.
82._accuracy_note: Good parallel on the moral priority of eating together; the Akbar episode is reported by Britannica as something 'said' by tradition, and the rule concerns communal equality rather than a host's private meal.

83.quote_or_event: “The Siblings of Destiny meet together, and eat and spend, but these resources do not diminish; they continue to increase.”
83.explanation: Guru Arjan describes a treasure that grows the more it is shared and spent together; the hymn's treasure is the divine Name, though the image draws on the experience of shared food and wealth.
83.tie_back: Like the Kural's assurance that daily hospitality never ruins a household, Gurbani holds that what is shared is not exhausted but increases.
83.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 186, Raag Gauree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
83._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on sharing that does not deplete; the hymn's inexhaustible treasure is spiritual (the Name), not the material provisions of a hospitable house.

84.quote_or_event: “Balwand says that Khivi, the Guru's wife, is a noble woman, who gives soothing, leafy shade to all. She distributes the bounty of the Guru's Langar; the kheer - the rice pudding and ghee, is like sweet ambrosia.”
84.explanation: The minstrels Satta and Balwand, in a ballad included in the Guru Granth Sahib, praise Mata Khivi, wife of Guru Angad, for the warmth with which she ran the langar and the abundance it gave everyone.
84.tie_back: As the Kural says Fortune dwells in the house of one who welcomes guests gladly, the scripture pictures plenty flowing from a household mistress whose welcome was shade to all.
84.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 967, Raag Raamkalee (Ramkali ki Vaar), Satta and Balwand (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
84._accuracy_note: Strong match on gracious hospitality and abundance, without the Kural's goddess of prosperity; the verse praises Khivi's generosity rather than promising wealth as its reward.

85.quote_or_event: “Make good deeds the soil, and let the Word of the Shabad be the seed; irrigate it continually with the water of Truth.”
85.explanation: Guru Nanak turns farming into a picture of the moral life, in which good conduct is the field that yields the true harvest.
85.tie_back: Like Valluvar's field that needs no sowing for the man who feeds guests first, it treats right action itself as the sowing that brings the crop.
85.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 24, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
85._accuracy_note: Partial fit: shares the agricultural image of deeds as the field, but says nothing of feeding guests first or eating what remains.

86.quote_or_event: “In the midst of this world, do seva, and you shall be given a place of honor in the Court of the Lord.”
86.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that selfless service (seva) done in ordinary worldly life earns a seat of honour in God's presence.
86.tie_back: As the Kural's perfect host becomes a welcome guest of the gods, the one who serves here is given a seat in the divine court.
86.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 26, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
86._accuracy_note: Strong structural parallel (service on earth answered by honour in the hereafter); seva is broader than hospitality and lacks the Kural's image of watching the road for the next guest.

87.quote_or_event: “Recognize the Lord's Light within all, and do not consider social class or status; there are no classes or castes in the world hereafter.”
87.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that every person carries the divine Light, so worth is never to be judged by caste or social rank, a principle the langar puts into practice by serving all alike.
87.tie_back: Where the Kural says the merit of hospitality is measured by the guest's worth, Gurbani locates every guest's worth in the same divine Light.
87.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 349, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
87._accuracy_note: Next-best only, partly a contrast: the Kural grades the fruit of hospitality by the guest's merit, while Sikh teaching refuses to rank recipients and sees the same Light in all.

88.quote_or_event: “For the sake of this wealth, so many were ruined; because of this wealth, so many have been disgraced. It was not gathered without sin, and it does not go along with the dead.”
88.explanation: In an Aasaa hymn, Guru Nanak reflects on hoarded wealth that brings its owners ruin and cannot be carried beyond death.
88.tie_back: It echoes the late lament of the Kural's hoarders, who toiled to guard their goods and are left with nothing to hold.
88.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
88._accuracy_note: Strong fit on the futility of hoarding, but the hymn does not set it against hospitality as the alternative the hoarder failed to choose.

89.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, those houses in which neither the Holy nor the Lord are served - those houses are like cremation grounds; demons dwell within them.”
89.explanation: In one of his saloks in the Guru Granth Sahib, Kabir says a household that does not serve holy visitors is spiritually dead, whatever it possesses.
89.tie_back: Like Valluvar's poverty in the midst of plenty, a house that fails to serve those who come to it is counted as empty and lifeless.
89.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1374, Salok Kabir (salok 192) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
89._accuracy_note: Strong fit on the household that fails in hospitality being inwardly destitute; Kabir's guests are specifically the Holy, and he speaks of spiritual death rather than folly.

90.quote_or_event: “Do not utter even a single harsh word; your True Lord and Master abides in all. Do not break anyone's heart; these are all priceless jewels.”
90.explanation: Sheikh Farid teaches that every heart is a priceless jewel in which God dwells, so even one harsh word or slight can shatter it.
90.tie_back: It shares the Kural's sense of how fragile the guest is: like the anicham flower, a heart can be wounded by a cold word or look alone.
90.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 129) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
90._accuracy_note: Good fit on the fragility of the heart; Farid speaks of harsh words toward anyone, not specifically of a host's averted face toward a guest.
